name: Mary Jean Price Walls
where: Missouri State campus, south of the Plaster Student Union
teaser: The first Black student to apply to Missouri State, turned away in 1950.
story: In 1950, Mary Jean Price was the salutatorian of her class and fully qualified when she became the first Black student to apply to what is now Missouri State University. The college denied her admission because of her race. Sixty years later, in 2010, the university awarded her an honorary bachelor's degree, and in 2016 it named the Mary Jean Price Walls Multicultural Resource Center Annex in her honor. She died in 2020. Her marker faces the center that carries her name.

name: Kentwood Arms Hotel
where: Kentwood Hall, 700 E. St. Louis St.
teaser: A Route 66 grand hotel that desegregated in 1960, then reversed course in 1962.
story:
Built in 1926 by local developer John T. Woodruff, the five-story Kentwood Arms on Route 66 quickly became a social and cultural landmark, hosting guests such as President Harry Truman, Bob Hope and Groucho Marx. It was also a segregated hotel.

In 1960, during Richard Nixon's campaign stop as vice president, Republican officials warned that Nixon would cancel his visit if the two Black members of the press traveling with him were denied lodging, and the local NAACP threatened to picket the hotel. City leaders decided to open public accommodation to everyone, and owner Earl Moulder announced the hotel's permanent desegregation. Other businesses, including Heer's department store, followed. In 1962, Moulder reversed course, claiming Springfield was “not quite ready.” The reversal reignited protests, and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 ultimately outlawed racial discrimination in public accommodations.

Southwest Missouri State University bought the building in 1984. Today it is Kentwood Hall.

name: Park Central Square
meta: Placed with the Equal Justice Initiative
teaser: Where the 1906 Easter lynchings took place.
story:
On Good Friday, April 13, 1906, Springfield and Greene County had a thriving population of African American professionals, business owners and community leaders. By the early hours of Easter Sunday, a false allegation that two Black men, Horace B. Duncan and Fred Coker, had assaulted a white woman had turned into a lynch mob. The two men had been taken to the city jail for their protection, where a third young Black man, William Allen, was already being held. The mob broke into the jail, took Mr. Duncan and Mr. Coker to the city square and hanged them from the Gottfried Tower, an iron structure topped with a replica of the Statue of Liberty. Then it returned to the jail for Mr. Allen and lynched him too. A crowd of thousands watched.

Fearing further violence, many African Americans left the city, some never to return. A grand jury indicted eighteen men who were involved. One man was brought to trial, but no one was ever convicted of these murders.

sections.title: Lynching in America
sections.kicker: Marker, side B · Equal Justice Initiative, 2019
sections.text:
Thousands of black people were the victims of lynching in the United States between 1877 and 1950. The lynching of African Americans during this era was a form of racial terrorism intended to intimidate black people and enforce racial hierarchy and segregation. After the Civil War, violent resistance to equal rights for African Americans led to fatal violence against black women, men, and children accused of violating social customs, engaging in interracial relationships, or committing crimes. Community leaders who spoke against this violence were themselves often targeted by mobs.

Racial lynching became the most public and notorious form of subordination directed at black people and was frequently tolerated or even supported by law enforcement and elected officials. White mobs were usually permitted to engage in brutal violence with impunity. Many black people were pulled out of jails or given over to mobs by law enforcement officials who were legally required to protect them. Lynchings often included burnings and mutilation, sometimes in front of crowds numbering in the thousands. Many of the victims of these acts of violence were not recorded by name and remain unknown, but over 50 lynchings have been documented in Missouri alone, with at least three having taken place in Greene County.
sections.status: Transcribed from the old trail website; not yet checked against the marker (no photo of side B).

videos.title: Community Remembrance Coalition Soil Collection Ceremony
videos.summary: Members of Springfield's Community Remembrance Coalition, the Springfield NAACP and representatives of the Black Archives of Mid-America in Kansas City collect and archive soil from the site on Park Central Square where Horace Duncan, Fred Coker and Will Allen were lynched in 1906.

name: Milly Sawyers
teaser: An enslaved woman who sued for her freedom in the 1830s, and won.
story:
Milly Sawyers, an enslaved African American woman, had lived in Ohio, a state that outlawed slavery, and argued that this made her free. She lost freedom suits in 1829 and 1833. In 1834 she was sold to Greene County resident William Ivey, and later that year she petitioned the court again, in what was possibly one of the first cases ever heard in Greene County circuit court. In August 1835 the court ruled that she was a free woman.

On April 1, 1836, a mob that included John P. Campbell, the founder of Springfield, broke into John Edwards' home at the northwest corner of Boonville Avenue and Olive Street, forced Sawyers onto the street and brutally beat her. She survived. Members of the mob were charged with rioting and assault, though the verdict remains unknown.

Her court papers sat forgotten until Greene County archivist Connie Yen came across them in 2017. The marker stands near the place where Sawyers was assaulted.

name: Alberta's Hotel
where: 625 N. Benton Ave., in front of the Springfield Municipal Court building
teaser: A safe place to stay for Black travelers on the Mother Road.
story: During segregation, Black travelers on Route 66 could not count on finding a room. Alberta's Hotel offered one, a safe place to stay in a city where most hotels turned them away. It is one of three markers on the trail tied to the Mother Road, alongside the Kentwood Arms and Graham's Rib Station.

name: Church Square South
teaser: Gibson Chapel Presbyterian and Pitts Chapel United Methodist, both founded in 1865.
story:
Two of Springfield's oldest Black congregations stand here. Gibson Chapel Presbyterian began in 1865 as the First Negro Cumberland Presbyterian Church, founded by Rev. Peter Lair (later Lear), a formerly enslaved man.

In 1891, a new brick church was built on the corner of Washington Avenue and Pine (now 536 E. Tampa Street). The church was renamed Gibson Chapel after the death of Reverend H. A. Gibson, who worked tirelessly to get the new structure erected. After the lynching of three innocent black men on the public square on Easter weekend, 1906, many families sought shelter in the chapel's basement while male church members guarded the building. The building was heavily damaged by fires in 1915 and 1935, but was rebuilt both times. After World War II, five members of the choir formed the singing group the Philharmonics. The group went on to regional and national fame.

Pitts Chapel United Methodist also dates to 1865, rebuilt after an arsonist burned its log church on Jordan Creek. Land donated by Fleming McCullah gave it a new home that also housed the Freedmen's Bureau school and, later, the public school for Black children. The congregation built its present church in 1911.

name: Church Square North
where: Central St., behind Benton Avenue AME
teaser: Completing the square of four historic Black churches.
story:
The north side of the church square honors two congregations, both founded in 1867. Benton Avenue African Methodist Episcopal Church stands at North Benton Avenue and East Central Street; its current building was completed in 1926 and placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2001. In 1959 the church welcomed Rev. Oliver L. Brown, the lead plaintiff in Brown v. Board of Education.

Washington Avenue Baptist Church began as a mission of the white First Baptist Church. Many Lincoln School educators were among its members and leaders, and in the 1960s and early 1970s its pastor, Rev. William E. Pitts, and its members worked with the NAACP and the Civil Rights Movement in Springfield. In 2000 the congregation moved to North National Avenue, and Drury University moved the historic church building brick by brick 300 feet north and restored it as a Diversity Center.

name: Graham's Rib Station
teaser: Barbecue and guest cabins for travelers on Route 66.
story:
In 1932, Zelma and James Graham opened The Rib Station at the corner of Washington Avenue and Chestnut Street. In the 1940s they built six stone cottages nearby, which became Graham's Modern Tourist Court. Chestnut Street was a Route 66 bypass, and many travelers stopped to eat and to sleep.

For 35 years, until it closed in 1967, the restaurant was a social hub for Springfield's African-American community. Famous entertainers ate and stayed at Graham's, including Duke Ellington, Pearl Bailey, Lionel Hampton, Louis Bellson and Harry Belafonte.

name: Lincoln School
where: OTC Lincoln Hall, N. Sherman Ave.
teaser: Springfield's high school for Black students until desegregation.
story: Until desegregation in 1955, this was Lincoln School, where Springfield's Black students went to high school. Its teachers anchored the neighborhood well beyond the classroom; one of them, Gerald Brooks, helped start the Park Day tradition at Silver Springs. The building lives on today as Ozarks Technical Community College's Lincoln Hall.

oralHistories.title: Richard's Story
oralHistories.speaker: Richard Lewis
oralHistories.summary: Richard “Bucky” Lewis was born on the corner of Sherman and Central. He was taught at Lincoln High School by teachers including Adah Fulbright, and was one of three high school seniors to integrate Central High School.
oralHistories.credit: From The Journey Continues, Missouri State University

oralHistories.title: Norma's Story
oralHistories.speaker: Norma Duncan
oralHistories.summary: Norma Duncan grew up in Springfield and can recall its history in extraordinary detail, a gift she credits to her mother, an English teacher at Lincoln. She remembers how segregation shaped daily life, including a bus ride from Joplin when the driver ordered her to give up her seat to a white woman, and a white classmate from Central High School stood with her the rest of the way.
oralHistories.credit: From The Journey Continues, Missouri State University

name: Silver Springs Park
teaser: The only public park designated for Black residents during segregation.
story:
Established in 1918 on land known as the Fairbanks Pasture, Silver Springs was the city's only public park designated for Black residents during segregation.

The land was originally owned by Jonathan Fairbanks, superintendent of Springfield Public Schools in the early 1900s. On Easter Eve, 1906, Fairbanks opened his home as a safe place for Black residents who were frightened by an unruly mob that had lynched three Black men on the town square.

The park was also home to various sports leagues, including semi-pro baseball. In the 1930s, the WPA built fieldstone retaining walls and the first Silver Springs Pool, and lined the creek channel with rock.

In 1952, park supervisors Gerald Brooks, also a Lincoln School teacher, and Robert Wendell Duncan started a day of games and sports for young people here. It grew into the annual Park Day Reunion, which still brings families home on the first weekend in August, celebrated with a parade, beauty pageant, concerts and a barbeque picnic. Park Day provided the backdrop for the 1998 film Park Day, by director Sterling Macer Jr., who grew up here. The trail's first marker was unveiled here in 2018, the park's centennial.

“One of the goals of the whole project is to promote healing and appreciation for the African American community's past and present,” said Springfield Mayor Ken McClure in his 2018 State of the City address. “… We are making great strides forward in diversity and inclusion but we have a long ways to go.”

videos.title: Springfield-Greene County African-American Heritage Trail officially launched at Park Day 2018
videos.summary: At the annual Park Day Reunion at Silver Springs Park in August 2018, during the park's 100th anniversary year, the trail's organizers unveiled an artist's rendering of the trail's first marker.

name: Lincoln Memorial Cemetery
meta: Funded in part by the Community Foundation of the Ozarks
teaser: Resting place of generations of Black Springfield.
story:
Lincoln Memorial Cemetery is the resting place of generations of Springfield's Black community, the families who built its churches, schools and businesses. Many of the people whose stories are told along the trail rest here.

Located at Chestnut Expressway and Barnes Avenue since 1919, the cemetery contains about 1,200 graves, with gravestones dating back to the 1850s. To mark its 100th anniversary, its volunteer board of directors held a rededication ceremony, with new fencing around the cemetery and a new monument.

name: Bartley-Decatur Neighborhood Center
where: Bartley-Decatur Neighborhood Center, 918 E. Calhoun St.
teaser: Named in honor of the schoolteacher sisters who operated the daycare for nearly three decades.
story:
The building that houses the Bartley-Decatur Neighborhood Center was built in 1900. The structure originally served as a private residence. Throughout its history it has served a variety of purposes.

After a couple of decades of being a home it was acquired by a newly formed organization called the Springfield Colored Hospital Association. It became known as the Negro Clinic from that time on. In the 1940s, it became a Black veterans' convalescent home. In 1941 the organization renamed itself the Springfield Colored Welfare Association. In the 1960s, for a short period of time, it was the Calhoun Community Center. The building was soon to have a different purpose.

Mrs. Roberta Bartley and her sister, Olive Decatur, were both retired school teachers who wanted to continue working with children, especially the children of their former students. The sisters had both been teachers at the nearby Lincoln School, which was a school for Black students in the era of segregation. They were also very active in the community serving in a variety of organizations. When the schools were desegregated, they were able to find jobs in the previously all white classrooms as well. Ms. Decatur was one of the first black teachers to be able to secure these positions and taught at Jarrett and Parkview schools.

In the early 1970s, Bartley, with her love of children, opened a daycare, in part to continue serving local families. The sisters were devoted to the center and the children that it served. The center, known as Kiddie Kove, became a community anchor as it was utilized by many people. Many of the parents were beginning to pursue higher education and the center served as a community lifeline. The center served the community for almost 30 years. The organization ended in 1999. After the closing the building sat empty. It began to deteriorate.

Fortunately, a local nonprofit began an initiative to give this important building another chapter. That organization was the Sherman Avenue Project Area Committee, a 501(c)(3) non-profit formed in the early 1990s to address housing issues. They also wanted to do something to save the former Kiddie Kove building. Having convened meetings of community members in the fall of 2002, the group decided to form a new nonprofit organization.

The organization was incorporated January 27, 2003 and named the Bartley-Decatur Neighborhood Center (BDNC), in honor of the schoolteacher sisters who operated the daycare for nearly three decades. BDNC was awarded a five hundred thousand dollar grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to reclaim and revitalize the building. The newly renovated building opened Park Day weekend (the first weekend in August) 2011.

Today the building is a hub for nonprofit activity serving primarily as a place where different organizations have been able to come together for meetings and programming.

These organizations have included ALAS (the Alliance for Leadership and Success), Celebrate Life and Unity in Our Community, Grupo Latinoamericano, Lincoln Cemetery Board, Springfield Reunion Club, the Springfield NAACP Chapter and Ujima Language and Literacy, among others.

Mark A. Dixon, Executive Director states the vision for Bartley-Decatur Neighborhood Center is clear and unwavering; to continue the legacy of the ladies and the work they started which he sees as education and continuing community impact. It serves as a place of collaboration, important conversation and placemaking.

He says “This building has served that community for over 100 years now and continues to do so.”
